summary:
Uttarakhand has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own. The national framework of India governs encounters with police, identity documents and public services in the state, and nothing in the sourced record shows a divergent state policy.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, narrowing the 2019 law. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 26 March 2026, states that the amendment removes self-identification, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification of identity, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification. The bill adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender; HRW warns that this could criminalise support networks. Of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, about 32,500 hold identity cards. HRW urged the president not to sign the bill, and assent was pending as of late March 2026.

BBC reporting of the same date records that recognition now rests on biological or physical traits alongside traditional identities, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment is a national change, so its effects reach Uttarakhand through the same route as every other state: recognition, certification and access to welfare schemes are now conditioned on membership of historically accepted socio-cultural groups or intersex status. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking.

Uttarakhand is not among the states named as operating transgender welfare boards. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha coordinate housing subsidies, surgery and pensions through such bodies, so a visitor comparing state-level provision should expect the Uttarakhand position to rest on national schemes rather than a state board.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented at transport hubs and border posts rather than in any single state: an airport identity check in Chennai in November 2024, a railway station gender check in Kolkata, custody treatment in Assam, and a passport medical-exam demand resolved by the Allahabad High Court in February 2026. The pattern is spread across jurisdictions, which is what makes it a national rather than local expectation.

Two credible assessments of police conduct point in opposite directions. A United Kingdom country policy note of December 2025 finds abuse limited and not systemic, while victim interviews of June 2024 document abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Both describe the same national environment.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any Uttarakhand-specific enforcement data, arrest figures, state welfare board or documented incident involving a trans person in the state. Whether Uttarakhand operates a state-level transgender welfare board is not stated in the inventory and remains unresolved.

Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was pending as of late March 2026; the inventory does not record a later assent date, commencement date or any transitional arrangement for identity documents already issued under the 2019 regime.
